applause: ( Applause and a couple of whistles fill the studio. )
( Big applause. Somebody throws something. It's fine. )
( The audience rises, a few of them, anyway. )
( Applause rolls in like it owes the room money. )
( Wild applause; a chair gives out; the show goes on. )
applause_guest: ( The crowd claps {guest} out to the chair. )
( The crowd stands for {guest}, then remembers the seats cost extra and sits. )
applause_host: ( The audience erupts as {host} strolls out. )
( The audience claps {host} out, half of them checking the exits first. )
( The band hits a sting and {host} walks into it like he owns the floor. )
audience: ( The audience laughs. )
( A big laugh rolls through the studio. )
( Scattered laughter, then a groan. )
( The crowd groans, then claps anyway. )
( Someone in the back whoops. )
( Nervous laughter. )
( A single, delayed "HA!" from the balcony. )
( The audience oooohs. )
( Laughter, and one heckler getting shushed. )
( Uneasy chuckles. )
( The audience absolutely loses it. )
( A polite ripple of laughter. )
( Someone claps once, loudly, alone. )
( Half the crowd laughs; the other half checks the exits. )
( A cough. One brave cough. )
( The audience laughs harder than the joke earned. )
( The audience gasps, then laughs at itself for gasping. )
( A long silence, then one person applauds out of politeness. )
( Genuine laughter, the good kind, the rare kind. )
( The crowd boos, warmly. )
( Someone yells "TOO SOON!" Someone else yells "NEVER SOON ENOUGH!" )
( Laughter, and the distinct sound of someone leaving. )
( The audience murmurs, unsure if that was allowed. )
( A wave of laughter, cut short by a flicker of the lights. )
( The room laughs, then goes quiet fast, the way people do here. )
( A big laugh. Somebody in the third row is crying and it is not clear why. )
( One long, low groan from four hundred people at once. )
( Laughter, then applause, then more laughter, in that order. )
( The crowd whoops. The band hits a sting. )
( Somebody shouts a name. It is not anybody's name. )
( Applause from one side of the studio only. )
( The audience laughs; a light fixture sways in agreement. )
( A hard laugh, cut off by a cough that goes on too long. )
( Delighted, appalled laughter. )
( The crowd thinks about it, then laughs late. )
( Two people laugh. Then everybody laughs at those two. )
( A whoop, a whistle, and a chant that is abandoned immediately. )
( The audience claps in that slow sarcastic way, then normally. )
( Somebody boos. Somebody else deals with it. Order restored. )
( Laughter with an edge on it. )
( The crowd howls. )
( A murmur of recognition, which is worse than a laugh and lands harder. )
( Silence, and then, from the balcony, one word: "Yeah." )
( The audience applauds a joke that has not finished landing. )
( Groans, and then applause for the groan. )
( The audience laughs. Somewhere behind them, a door closes. )
( One person laughs alone for a long time and nobody stops them. )
( The room goes up. The floor manager makes a signal nobody understands. )
( A laugh, a beat, and then the room works out what he said. )
( Applause, some of it from the band. )
( The audience says "awww" and means none of it. )
( Laughter, and one person applauding with a single hand. )
( A shocked laugh from the front row and nothing at all from the back. )
( The crowd laughs, and keeps laughing, and has to be brought back. )
( A groan that turns into a cheer halfway through. )
( Somebody laughs like a door hinge. It gets a bigger laugh than the joke. )
( The room laughs. Somewhere in it, one man does not. )
( Applause that starts before the punchline and has to commit. )
( The audience winces, then laughs at the wince. )
( A laugh, and then the sound of four hundred people deciding not to think about it. )
( Warm laughter. It is nice in here. It will not last. )
( The crowd goes very still, and then breaks. )
( Laughter, a whistle, and a small crash offstage that nobody acknowledges. )
( The audience laughs at the wrong part, which is somehow better. )
banter: {host_first}, I have to ask: do you write these yourself? >> Every word, {sidekick_first}. >> That explains a great deal, and I'd like to stop thinking about it.
{host_first}, the audience has questions. >> About the show? >> About the exits, mostly. I gave them what I knew.
I've been told to remind you we're live, {host_first}. >> I know we're live, {sidekick_first}. >> You didn't sound like a man who knew that. I'm just doing my job.
{host_first}, your microphone is fine. >> I didn't ask about my microphone. >> I know. I wanted you to have one piece of good news tonight.
Can I say something, {host_first}? >> Can I stop you? >> No. That's the arrangement. That's been the arrangement since the fire.
{host_first}, I looked up your contract today. >> And? >> And it's beautiful work, {sidekick_first}. Not the contract. The looking up. It took me eleven minutes to find where they'd hidden it.
The band has a request, {host_first}. >> Music? >> Distance. They'd like more of it, between them and the desk.
{host_first}, I want you to know the crowd is with you. >> That's kind, {sidekick_first}. >> Physically. They're locked in until eleven. But they're with you.
I've done the arithmetic, {host_first}. >> On what? >> On how many of those we have left before the network intervenes. It's fewer than you'd like and more than I'd hoped.
{host_first}, quick note from the booth. >> Go ahead. >> They've asked whether you could do the show slightly differently. >> Differently how? >> They didn't specify. I think that's the note.
You know what I admire about you, {host_first}? >> Tell me. >> The confidence. Not the material. I want to be precise, because the lawyers are.
{host_first}, be honest with me. >> Always, {sidekick_first}. >> Do you enjoy this? >> Not for a moment. >> Good. It shows, and I'd hate to think you were hiding it.
I've got a card here from the producers, {host_first}. >> Read it. >> It says "keep going." That's all it says. It's not encouragement, {host_first}, it's an instruction.
{host_first}, the crowd's warm tonight. >> They are. >> They're warm because the air handling failed. But I know how much you needed that.
Something's different about you tonight, {host_first}. >> New suit. >> That's it. I thought you'd slept.
{host_first}, I'd like to register a formal objection. >> To what? >> I'll fill in the details later. I wanted it timestamped before whatever you're about to say.

desk_bit: Now, before we bring out our guest, you're not going to believe what I saw on the way in tonight.
Speaking of terrible decisions, let me tell you about my week. Actually, let me not. Legal's here.
Here's something. We got a letter from a viewer tonight. It was a threat, but it was very neatly written, so: progress.
You know what I love about this city? Nothing. But I love saying it, and that's the same thing after a while.
Quick programming note: if the screen goes dark for a moment, that's not us, that's the grid, and there is nothing anyone can do.
We tried a new thing this week where we told the truth for a full minute. We got fined. We're not doing that again.
I want to thank our sponsors, all of whom are currently under investigation, which is how you know they can afford us.
So the network gave me "notes" this week. The main note was "fewer notes." I'm choosing to honor that spiritually.
Somebody in the front row is eating during my monologue. Sir. This is a comedy program. Show some fear.
Little behind-the-scenes for you: the desk isn't real. None of it's real. The desk is the most real thing here and it's cardboard.
Little housekeeping: if you hear an alarm during the show, finish watching first. It's rude to leave during the good part.
I got recognized on the street today. By a bounty drone. We had a lovely chat and then I ran.
We got a new intern this week. Brave kid. Started Monday, filed a missing-persons report on himself Wednesday, just to be safe.
Somebody asked why we still do the show live. Because taped means they'd have time to stop us. Live means they have to catch up.
The network wanted me to plug the new app. It tracks your every move. I said mine already does that, it's called the rent.
Real quick: happy anniversary to my landlord and me. Ten years. He still doesn't fix the heat, I still don't pay on time. Longest relationship I've got.
greeting: {sidekick_first}. You look well. >> I look EMBALMED, {host_first}. But thank you for saying it in front of witnesses.
How are we doing tonight, {sidekick_first}? >> Alive, employed, and only one of those by choice.
{sidekick_first}, good crowd tonight. >> It's a crowd, {host_first}. "Good" is a scheduling matter.
Nineteen years, {sidekick_first}. Nineteen years we've done this. >> And every one of them, {host_first}, you've asked me that like it's a surprise.
{sidekick_first}, did you do anything nice this week? >> I slept, {host_first}. Through a fire alarm. Best night I've had in months.
Talk to me, {sidekick_first}. How's the building? >> Standing. Ask me again after the second commercial.
{sidekick_first}, were you here for rehearsal? >> I was here for rehearsal, {host_first}. I'd like that considered at my sentencing.
You're quiet tonight, {sidekick_first}. >> I'm PACED, {host_first}. There's a lot of show left and only one of us is being paid by the hour.
{sidekick_first}, tell the people what we've got coming. >> A guest, a sponsor, and roughly eleven minutes of you, {host_first}. Brace accordingly.
Good to see you, {sidekick_first}. >> You saw me forty minutes ago, {host_first}. You were crying. We agreed not to mention it.
{sidekick_first}, how was your commute? >> Two checkpoints and a man who wanted to sell me my own coat back.
{sidekick_first}, anything I should know before we start? >> Several things, {host_first}. None of them survivable. Let's do the show.

guest_noshow: {sidekick_first}. There's no one in the chair. >> I see the chair, {host_first}. I've been looking at the chair for some time now.
Where is our guest, {sidekick_first}? >> In transit, {host_first}. That's the word the booth used. It's a generous word. It covers a great deal of ground and several outcomes.
{sidekick_first}, did we book a guest tonight? >> We booked one. We are between the booking and the guest. It's a wide space and people do get lost in it.
So what do we do now, {sidekick_first}? >> What we always do, {host_first}. We talk until something happens. It's worked before. Twice.
Is anyone looking for them? >> Two interns and a drone, {host_first}. The drone is the one I'd bet on.
{sidekick_first}, I've interviewed empty chairs before. >> You have. And I'd like the record to show the chair came off better both times.
Should I be worried, {sidekick_first}? >> About the guest? No. About the twelve minutes of airtime we've just inherited? Yes, {host_first}, and immediately.
{sidekick_first}, what do we know? >> That they left. That they were coming here. Everything after that is theology.
This has happened before, hasn't it? >> Four times this year, {host_first}. Three came back. We don't discuss the fourth on air.
Can we just go to the commercial? >> The commercial is ninety seconds, {host_first}. You'd still be sitting here afterwards, and so would the chair.
{sidekick_first}, say something reassuring. >> The building is insured. >> That's not reassuring. >> It's what I've got, {host_first}. The rest is aspiration.

All right. {sidekick_first}, YOU sit in the chair. >> I will not. >> Why not? >> Because then there'd be nobody to announce you, {host_first}, and you'd be entirely alone up here. Think about that carefully before you ask again.
host_absent: Ladies and gentlemen... he isn't here. I've announced that man for nineteen years and tonight I've announced him to a chair.
The booth is telling me to stall. I've been stalling since "ladies and gentlemen." I'm out of ladies and I'm out of gentlemen.
I want to be straight with you, because you stayed up: there's no host tonight, and I'm not going to stand here and do his half badly.
I could tell you a joke. I've heard nineteen years of them. That is not the same as being able to tell one.
Somebody will ask why I didn't just carry it. Because it's his show. My job is to say his name and mean it, and I can't do that to an empty desk.
The chair's warm. Not from him. From the lights. I checked. I'd checked before I said it, which tells you how the night's gone.
Nineteen years I've needled that man for being late. I'd like the record to show I would take it all back for one entrance.
We're going to go to a break, and then we're going to go home. There is no version of this where I sit in that chair.
He's not answering. The booth isn't answering. The generator's answering, so at least you can watch me not know things in good light.
Whatever's happened to him, he'd want me to fill. He'd be wrong about that, and it would be the second thing tonight he was wrong about.
To whoever's still watching at this hour: thank you. That's not a bit. You came for him and you got me, and you stayed anyway.
host_absent_signoff: That's the show, such as it was. I'm {sidekick}, and I only ever wanted to say somebody else's name. Goodnight.
We'll be back tomorrow, and so will he, and I'll pretend none of this happened. Goodnight from KSAB.
Go to bed. That's the whole broadcast. Go to bed and we'll try it again tomorrow with the full complement.
That's KSAB, signing off a show that didn't start. Get home safe. Somebody should.
Goodnight. If you see him out there, tell him the audience waited. Tell him I waited too, but lead with the audience.
interview: [arrival] Welcome to the show. First off: are you okay? You can blink twice. >> I've survived worse rooms than this one, {host_first}. Barely.
[arrival] Let's start easy: how was the trip in? >> Two checkpoints, one shakedown, and a man selling maps to the exit. Standard, {host_first}.
[arrival] Did our people treat you well backstage? >> They gave me a form, a bottle of water, and a look. I've signed the form. I'm still thinking about the look.
[sleep] Be honest with me: do you sleep at night? >> Like a baby. I wake up every two hours screaming. Same as everyone in this city.
[sleep] What keeps you up at night? >> The ceiling, mostly. It's structural. But also, yes, the dread.
[sleep] How do you unwind after a long day? >> I sit very still in the dark and let the building settle. If it settles quietly, I've won.
[misconception] What's the biggest misconception about what you do? >> That I know what I'm doing. I do not. Nobody does. That's the whole secret.
[misconception] What's the one thing people always get wrong about you? >> They think I chose this. I was ASSIGNED this. There's a difference, and there's a form.
[regret] Last question, our lawyers are standing: would you do it all again? >> {host_first}, I'm contractually obligated to do it again. Twice, on weekends.
[regret] Any regrets? >> Regret's a luxury, {host_first}. I can barely afford the studio parking.
[career] What would you tell young people considering your line of work? >> Aim low. That way the disappointment is punctual.
[career] Did you always know this was your calling? >> I knew the day everyone told me to stop. That's usually the sign, isn't it?
[career] So how did you even get started? >> One bad decision, made confidently, repeated until it became a career.
[career] Any advice you wish someone had given you? >> "Don't." One word. Would've saved everyone a lot of paperwork, including yours.
[career] What would you be doing if not this? >> The same thing, {host_first}, but without the title and the dental. Mostly I'm here for the dental.
[career] Ever think about quitting? >> Every morning. Then the alarm goes off, and by "alarm" I mean the neighbors, and by "morning" I mean it's still dark.
[money] And the money. As good as they say? >> It's incredible. It's also on fire, and so are my hands. But it's incredible.
[money] Do you ever worry about money? >> I've stopped, {host_first}. Not because it improved. Because worrying was the last thing I owned outright and I sold it.
[mentor] Who taught you all this? >> A mentor. Then he vanished. I like to think he retired. The evidence suggests otherwise.
[reputation] People either love you or fear you. Which do you prefer? >> Fear's more reliable, {host_first}. Love expects things back.
[reputation] Do people recognize you on the street? >> They recognize the liability, {host_first}. The face comes second.
[rumors] There are rumors. Care to set the record straight? >> They're mostly true, and the parts that aren't, I'm flattered by.
[bestworst] Best part of the job, worst part, go. >> Same part, {host_first}. That's the trouble with an honest living out here.
[bestworst] Be honest: is it as bad as it looks? >> No, {host_first}. It's worse. But it looks bad from a very flattering angle tonight.
[routine] What's a normal day look like for you? >> There are no normal days. There's the day it works and the day it's on the news. Sometimes both.
[family] Do your parents know what you do? >> My mother thinks I'm in "logistics." She's not entirely wrong, and I'd like to keep it that way.
[danger] What's the most dangerous part of the job? >> The commute, easily. The job itself is only trying to kill me part-time.
[rivals] Do you have any rivals? >> I had one. We settled our differences. He settled first. It was very amicable, geographically speaking.
[pride] What's your proudest achievement? >> I'm still here, {host_first}. In this city, that's not a milestone, that's a miracle with a pulse.
[machine] If you could tell the Machine one thing, what would it be? >> Nothing. It's listening right now. Hi. We're all very productive. Please don't.
[city] What would you change about this city? >> Nothing, {host_first}. Every single thing here is load-bearing. Pull one out and we all learn something we can't unlearn.
[city] Would you ever leave the Basin? >> And go where? I've read the map. It's the same map, {host_first}. They just print it in different colours.
[future] Where do you see yourself in five years? >> That's a beautiful question and I'd like you to hear how funny it is out loud. Five years.
[fear] What actually frightens you? >> Paperwork that arrives without being requested. Everything else in this city announces itself first.
[trust] Who do you trust? >> One person, {host_first}. I won't say who, and I'd appreciate it if the camera stopped doing that.
[lucky] Do you consider yourself lucky? >> I consider myself OVERDUE. Those look identical from the outside and they are not the same thing.
[first] Tell me about your first day. >> I've been told not to. Not by lawyers. By a friend, which is worse, because a friend has no reason to lie about it.
[worstday] What's the worst day you've had on this job? >> Tuesday. >> Which Tuesday? >> That's the trouble, {host_first}. That's exactly the trouble.
[health] How's your health, if you don't mind me asking? >> The clinic says I'm in the top percentile. They wouldn't say of what, or of whom, and the room got quiet.
[secret] Is there anything you've never told anyone? >> Several things, {host_first}, and I've kept them alive this long by not doing what you're currently inviting me to do.
[retire] Any plans to retire? >> In my line of work, {host_first}, retirement isn't a plan. It's a verdict, and somebody else reads it out.
[fame] Has any of this gone to your head? >> It went straight past my head, {host_first}. It's been going around behind me for years and I've stopped turning to look.
[food] What's the last decent meal you had? >> Define decent. >> Something that didn't move. >> Then I'd have to check my notes, and I'd rather we both didn't.
[love] Anyone special in your life? >> There was. She read the job description. That was the end of a very promising evening.
interview.assemblyman: You think the Assembly should govern something. That's an unusual position. >> It's lonely, {host_first}. They seat me near the door so I can't block the exits.
What are you working on? >> A bill to fix the potholes on Foundry Way. It's been in committee four years. The potholes have done better.
Do your colleagues like you? >> They like me the way you like a smoke alarm, {host_first}. In principle.
Would you ever run for something bigger? >> I'd need somebody to vote for me. I've got my mother and a man who thinks I'm somebody else.
What would you change first, if you could? >> I'd make the Assembly meet. Just meet. In the same room, once. Then we'd see.
interview.barkeep: The Dead Pigeon. Why a pigeon? >> It was there when I bought the place, {host_first}. Still is, in a manner of speaking.
Your bar's a door on two oil drums. Ever think about a proper one? >> A proper bar gets taken in a raid. Nobody confiscates a door.
You must hear a lot of sob stories. >> All of them, twice. I can tell you how most of them end. I don't, because they tip better before.
What's the most popular drink at the Pigeon? >> Whatever's cheapest. Then whatever's second cheapest, when they find out why.
Do you ever drink at your own bar? >> Once. I paid. It was the most honest night that place has ever had.
interview.bouncer: You're on the door at the Cherry. What's the job, really? >> Watching, {host_first}. Most nights you never move. You just make sure people see you not moving.
Is there anyone you always turn away? >> Same man every Friday. Nine years. He's never got in and he's never stopped trying. I respect him.
What's the secret to bouncing? >> Stand still and look bored. People can't stand being looked at by somebody bored.
Have you ever lost a fight? >> Once. I was off duty. It doesn't count, and I'd thank you not to bring it up.
What's the earpiece for? >> Mostly the bar telling me what they want for lunch.
interview.chef: These squid tacos. Are they safe? >> Probably fine, {host_first}. "Probably" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and I respect it.
Where do you source your ingredients? >> Locally. Out here that means "from a hole I don't fully understand."
People say your food's dangerous. >> My food is HONEST. The danger is a seasoning.
What's on the menu tonight? >> The special, {host_first}. I don't know what's in it either. That's why it's special.
Any Michelin interest? >> A man came, ate, left, and filed a report. Not a review. A report. I framed it.
interview.chippy: Batter Days. Who came up with the name? >> Not me. I just fry. I've been told it's a joke and I believe them.
What's the secret to good chips? >> Twice in the fat, and don't look at the fat.
Those are burn marks on your arms. >> Every one's a fish that fought back. I don't hold it against them.
Do you talk to the fryers? >> They listen better than the customers. They don't want it with a different sauce.
What's the best thing on the menu? >> The cod, when there's cod. When there isn't, it's called "today's fish", and it's still the best thing on the menu.
interview.colonel: Colonel, tell us about the war. >> I can neither confirm nor deny it, {host_first}. Officially, it didn't happen. I have a medal that says so.
And the pension? >> For a conflict in no record. I cash it monthly. The check is real. The war is "complicated."
What won it, in the end? >> Discipline. That's what won us the... well. Whatever it was we may or may not have won.
Colonel, did you have a rank? >> I had SEVERAL, {host_first}, all of them classified, some of them contradictory. I outranked myself twice.
Do you miss the service? >> I miss the certainty, {host_first}. Out here nobody tells you who to shoot. You have to guess. It's exhausting.
interview.cphl: [table] The {club} are {club_rank}, {club_record}. Fair? >> It's what the ice says, {host_first}. The ice doesn't lie. It just doesn't help.
[role] What's it actually like being {role_said} for the {club}? >> Mostly it's being the one they look at when it goes wrong. Which, out here, is most nights.
[vat] Be honest with me. Does the vat hurt? >> Only coming out. Going in, you're dead, so nobody asks your opinion.
[room] What's the dressing room like? >> Loud. Somebody's always just back from the vat, asking what they missed and who owes them money.
[ken] Do you ever talk to Ken Raven? >> Everybody talks to Ken. Ken waves. That's as far as it goes with Ken.
[fans] What do the fans shout at you? >> My name, mostly. Then what they'd like to do to me. It's nice to be thought of.
[rival] Who's the man you least want to see on the ice? >> The one I put in the vat last time. They come back remembering, {host_first}. The vat doesn't take that out.
interview.deadball: [season] How's the season been for you? >> {season}
[table] The {club} are {club_rank}, {club_record}. What's going on out there? >> Baseball, {host_first}. With the rules they took out put back in. It's going about how you'd expect.
[role] Being {role_said} for the {club}, is there pressure? >> There's a man in the stands with a sign that has my address on it. So yes.
[organ] Does the organ get to you? >> One song, nine innings, every night. I hum it in my sleep. My wife hums it back.
[name] Is the "dead" in Deadball literal? >> Some nights, {host_first}. The umpire has a page on it. Mostly it's a figure of speech that keeps happening.
[slide] What's the hardest thing about the game? >> Sliding. Into second there's a man with spikes, and into home there's a man with worse.
[fans] Do people recognise you on the street? >> They recognise the uniform. Then they tell me what I did wrong in the seventh, and they're usually right.
interview.enforcer: Eleven times through the vat. Does it get easier? >> The dying's the same, {host_first}. The paperwork's got a lot better.
What do you remember about the first fight? >> Nothing. That's the vat. I've seen the tape, though. I'd have hit me too.
Do you miss playing? >> I miss the crowd. I don't miss waking up in a tank asking what year it is.
Who was the toughest man you ever fought? >> Myself, {host_first}. The fourth one. The vat got the teeth wrong and he was furious about it.
Any advice for the young enforcers coming up? >> Keep your elbows in and your contract signed. Clubs don't pay for the vat if you're between deals.
Is it true you've got more teeth in a jar than in your head? >> Forty-one in the jar. Six in the head. Two of those are on loan.
interview.exorcist: An Undermarket exorcist. Is any of it real? >> Most "hauntings" are bad wiring, {host_first}. But the other ten percent? That's why I carry two staplers.
Is exorcism as dramatic as they say? >> It's mostly paperwork. The spirits, like everyone down there, just want to be seen.
And you're... licensed? >> I paid for the license. The demon that runs the licensing office was very reasonable.
What's the worst haunting you've handled? >> A vending machine, {host_first}. Possessed. Or maybe just Ophelia's. Down there you can't always tell.
Do the spirits ever win? >> One did, {host_first}. It owns a laundromat now. Pays taxes. Honestly, it assimilated better than most of us.
interview.florist: Flowers, out here. Where do you even get them? >> Greenhouses, mostly. Some come in on trucks. Some I don't ask about.
What sells best? >> Lilies for funerals. Roses for apologies. Carnations for people who don't mean either.
Your hands look cold. >> They've been cold for twenty years, {host_first}. Wet stock, cold room. You stop noticing.
Do you like your customers? >> I like the flowers. The customers are fine if they know what they want before they come in.
What's the worst order you've had? >> A wreath shaped like a man's ex-wife. He wanted it for her birthday. She's alive. I did it anyway.
interview.forecaster: Estes Maritime. How big is the company? >> It's me, {host_first}. It's a very lean operation.
You own a dozen ships. Have you seen them? >> Not personally. I've seen paperwork about them, and the paperwork is beautiful.
What's your call on freight this quarter? >> Up. I always say up. You'd be amazed how often something goes up.
On paper you're very rich. And off paper? >> I'm sitting in your chair because the coffee's free, {host_first}.
Any tips for the folks at home? >> Buy whatever I'm selling. Tomorrow it'll be worth more, or there'll be a reason it isn't.
interview.hoarder: Three-time hoarding champion. The secret? >> You never, ever, EVER let go. Of anything. Ever.
People call it a problem. >> The trophies call it a lifestyle, {host_first}. I have all three. And their boxes. And the receipts.
What's your proudest possession? >> The narrow path from my door to my chair. That path is my life's work.
What can't you throw away? >> Nothing, {host_first}. That's the sport. Last year I kept a sneeze. I have it in a jar. It's loyal.
Do you ever run out of room? >> Room is a myth the un-committed tell themselves, {host_first}. There's always room. You just have to love harder.
interview.icedriver: What's it like driving the Zamboni? >> It's quiet, {host_first}. Twenty thousand people screaming, and it's the quietest job in the city.
That Zamboni's had a paint job. >> That's mine, {host_first}. Black, purple, gold, my name down both sides. I did it for one Cup final and nobody's had the nerve to ask me to take it off.
They say you've never stopped for a fight. >> I'm on a schedule. If two grown men want to fight in front of four tonnes of machine, that's between them and the machine.
You're a Marrow Street boy, and a Marauders man. Is it hard to stay neutral? >> I do both ends the same, {host_first}. I just do the Marauders' end with a bit more love.
What's the secret to good ice? >> Patience, hot water, and not looking at what's frozen into it from last season.
Do the players talk to you? >> They wave. I wave back. It's the most honest relationship in the building.
What do you do between periods? >> I sit on the machine with the engine off and eat a sandwich. People think I'm guarding it. I'm eating a sandwich.
interview.influencer: Nine million followers. That's remarkable. >> Every one a bot I personally pay, {host_first}. Do you know how expensive authenticity is?
Isn't that just fake engagement? >> My bots have never let me down. Can you say that about a person?
Doesn't it ever feel hollow? >> I post my breakfast, the bots love it, I feel seen. The illusion holds one more day. It's the modern condition.
What's your engagement rate? >> One hundred percent, {host_first}. The bots never miss. That's more than I can say for my own family.
Ever meet a real follower? >> Once, {host_first}. It was terrifying. He had OPINIONS. My bots would never. I blocked reality that day.
interview.insurer: Vice-President of Everything Regrettable. What does that involve? >> Everything regrettable, {host_first}. You'd be amazed how much of the city that covers. Ninety floors of it, at least.
Is that a tan? There's no sun here. >> There is if you pay for the right floor.
What does Halcyon actually insure? >> Everything except what happens. That's in the small print, which is most of the print.
Has anyone ever made a successful claim? >> Twice. We've framed them both. They're in the lobby as a warning to the staff.
Can I get a quote, while you're here? >> You already have one, {host_first}. You got it when you walked out. It went up when you sat down.
interview.lawsuit: You're suing the sun? >> Emotional distress, {host_first}. It's been up there this whole time, judging me, and I've had enough.
What are your chances, realistically? >> My lawyer says it's a long shot, jurisdictionally. I said, so is the sun.
What happens if you win? >> Every sunrise owes me residuals. Think about the precedent. Think about the light.
Has the sun responded to the suit? >> It rose the next morning, {host_first}, which my lawyer says is either contempt or a confession. We're arguing which.
Any other defendants on your list? >> Gravity's next. It's been holding me down my whole life and it's never apologized.
interview.lucky: You've won the city lottery eight times. What's the secret? >> Always buy the ticket right after surviving something that should've killed you.
Eight jackpots. Do you at least feel lucky? >> I feel HUNTED, {host_first}. There's a difference, and the difference has a legal team.
What was the first thing you bought? >> A deluxe apartment. The deluxe part is that only one wall leaks.
Eight jackpots. Do the corporates let you keep it? >> They let me keep the STORY, {host_first}. The money went to "processing fees." All of it. Every time.
Any tips for the folks at home? >> Yeah, win eight times so they can't pin any single one on you. Amateurs get caught at four.
interview.monk: Brother Tobias, welcome. What brings you here tonight? >> ...
Can you tell us a little about the vow? >> ......
Anything at all you'd like to say to the folks at home? >> (a stare of profound, radiant, aggressive silence)
Brother Tobias. A nod for yes? >> (holds an aggressive, unbroken stare)
Anything for the young monks watching? >> (very slowly, and with menace, raises a single finger to his lips)
interview.nation: You declared your apartment a sovereign nation. How's governance? >> One law, one citizen, and a standing army of me holding a bat.
Any foreign relations? >> We've opened talks with 4B down the hall. It's tense. They have a working stove.
Do the corporates recognize your statehood? >> They don't, {host_first}. But they DO recognize my rent. So we're at an impasse.
Does your nation have a flag? >> A gray towel, {host_first}. It's what I had. It's also the ceiling situation, so some days it flies itself.
Any tourism? >> One visitor. The landlord. It became a hostage situation. We've since normalized relations.
interview.organist: You only know one song. Is that true? >> It's true, {host_first}. I know it very well, though. Nobody can say I don't.
What's the song about? >> Drowning. In D minor. The network made a theme out of it, and I've still not seen a cheque.
Have you ever tried to learn another one? >> Once. The crowd booed. They know where they are with the one.
Why not learn something cheerful? >> They're watching Deadball at the Hughson, {host_first}. Cheerful would upset them.
How do you know when to play it? >> When something happens. When nothing happens. Seventh inning. I'm flexible about everything except the song.
Do you play it at home? >> My wife asked me not to. So I play it in the car, with the windows down, so the whole street gets to share.
interview.pitboss: Why do they call you The Rake? >> I rake in the chips, {host_first}. It's a casino. People expected it to be more sinister. I let them.
What do you look for, watching the floor? >> Hands. The face lies, the hands don't. Yours have been in your pockets since you sat down.
Has anybody ever beaten the house at the Lucky Bastard? >> For a night. The house is very patient. It sends a car.
Do you gamble yourself? >> Never. I've seen how it ends from the good side of the table.
What's the best tell you've ever seen? >> A man who started crying before he looked at his cards. He was right to.
interview.priest: Father, how's the congregation at St Garneau's these days? >> Smaller, {host_first}. Steadier. The ones who come now mean it, or they've nowhere else warm.
Do you get many confessions? >> More than you'd think. Nobody in this city does anything once.
What's the hardest part of the job? >> Burying people I've already buried. The vat's made a mess of the calendar.
Do you ever lose your faith? >> Most Tuesdays. It comes back about the time somebody needs it more than I do.
You watch the door a lot, Father. >> Old habit. I knew this city when the door was the most important thing in the room.
interview.reverend: Tell us about the Church of the Reasonable Refund. >> We teach that suffering is real, {host_first}, and you're entitled to store credit for it.
Do you pass a collection plate? >> We pass a receipt. Salvation is itemized.
How's the flock these days? >> Grown to hundreds. Mostly people who wanted a refund and found God in the returns line.
What's a sermon like at the Church of the Reasonable Refund? >> I hold up a receipt, {host_first}, and the congregation weeps, because they remember what they paid.
Do miracles happen? >> A man got store credit approved on a final-sale item last spring. We're still talking about it. We built a small shrine.
interview.scavenger: You got rich off a toaster? >> One working toaster, {host_first}. In this economy, a machine that browns bread reliably is a small nation's GDP.
People laughed at scavenging for a living. >> Nobody's laughing from inside their leaking apartment.
Ever find anything stranger than the toaster? >> I don't talk about the doll. We don't talk about the doll, {host_first}.
Since the toaster, what's the market like? >> Cutthroat, {host_first}. Everybody's out there now with a stick, poking hope. I sold my stick. Retired.
Do you still scavenge? >> Only emotionally, {host_first}. I comb the past for anything I can still use. Slim pickings.
interview.sparky: From grid saboteur to safety consultant? >> Same job, {host_first}. I just bill for it now.
Do you feel guilty about the blackouts? >> I feel EMPLOYED. The blackouts built my client list.
What's the key to electrical safety? >> Respect the current. I did not, for years, and now I glow faintly.
What's the biggest blackout you take credit for? >> The Long Dark, {host_first}. Six districts. I don't talk about it, but I do put it on the invoice.
Any advice for homeowners? >> Don't touch the box, {host_first}. That's my box now. Everything's my box now. That's the consulting.
interview.surgeon: You run the clinic. What comes through the door on a bad night? >> Everything, {host_first}. Knives, chemicals, people who tried to fix their own wiring. Mostly the wiring.
Do people pay? >> When they can. When they can't, they bring something. I've got a shelf of things people brought.
What's the strangest thing you've taken out of somebody? >> A tracking chip, from a man who swore he'd never had one fitted. He hadn't. Somebody else had.
How do you stay calm? >> I've seen worse walk in, {host_first}. I've seen worse walk out, too, and that's the part that keeps me going.
Any advice for the viewers? >> Don't buy organs from a van. And if you do, come and see me before you plug anything in.
interview.taster: A professional poison taster. How are you still alive? >> Spite, mostly, {host_first}. And a truly world-class stomach lining.
Two livers, is that right? >> One and a half now. It's been a week.
Is it a rough gig? >> Ninety percent fine, ten percent the worst afternoon of your life. I've had a lot of afternoons.
What's the worst thing you've tasted? >> Tuesday, {host_first}. All of it. I tasted the whole day and I do not recommend it.
How do you know when something's poisoned? >> I don't, {host_first}. That's the JOB. I find out the way everyone does: dramatically, and on the floor.
interview.umpire: A perfect record. Is that true? >> Depends how you count, {host_first}. I count the calls nobody argued with, and nobody argues with me.
Why does nobody argue with you? >> They used to. Then the league gave me the mask with the speaker in it. It's very loud.
Have you ever got one wrong? >> Professionally, no. Personally, I married a Crows fan.
What's the hardest call in Deadball? >> Whether a man's dead or just resting. The rulebook's got a whole page on it and the page is mostly blood.
Do you have favourite teams? >> No. I hate them all the same, {host_first}. That's what makes me fair.
What do you do in the off-season? >> Same thing. I just stand in the kitchen and point at things. My family calls it out on the third strike.
interview.vending: Your machine has killed forty people. Care to comment? >> Forty lives, yes, but thousands of beverages dispensed. It's a NET positive.
Is the machine... okay? >> Legally it's a person now. Emotionally, it's a person very disappointed in all of us.
What do you call this business model? >> "Aggressive vending." "Killing spree" tested poorly with the beverage demographic.
What flavor does the machine dispense? >> "Original," {host_first}. Same as the funerals. We keep the branding consistent.
Is there a recall? >> There's a MEMORIAL, {host_first}. A recall implies the machine did something wrong, and legally, the machine is grieving.
list_bit: Tonight's top four signs your landlord is a cult. || Four: the rent is due on the solstice. || Three: the lease is in Latin, and so is the lawn. || Two: the super wears a robe and he has never once fixed anything. || And number one: you keep getting invited to the basement, and nobody comes back up with their deposit.
Three things you should never say to Corporate Security. || Three: "Do you have a warrant?" || Two: "I know my rights." || And number one: "Funny, you look just like the guy from last week."

Tonight's top three excuses for missing work in the Basin. || Three: the stairs were gone. || Two: the bus was on fire, and I was on the bus. || And number one: the Machine told me I didn't work there, and I didn't want to argue with it.

Four ways to tell the tap water's gone bad again. || Four: it's warm from the cold tap. || Three: it's got a taste, and the taste has a name. || Two: the glass is sweating, and it's nervous. || And number one: it comes out in one piece.
Tonight's top three things you'll hear at a Cluster Puck game. || Three: "Get him in the vat!" || Two: "He's fine, he's fine, he's not fine." || And number one: "Same man, different teeth."

Three signs you've been at Deadball too long. || Three: you know the organist's song and you hum it at funerals. || Two: you can tell a slide from a seizure. || And number one: the umpire knows your name and he's never once said it kindly.
Tonight's top three rejected slogans for the city. || Three: "Coldwater: We Have Walls." || Two: "Coldwater: Somewhere To Be From." || And number one: "Coldwater: Ask About Our Exits."

Four things you never want to hear from a surgeon in the Undermarket. || Four: "Hold this." || Three: "That's a new one." || Two: "Who's got the manual?" || And number one: "Nobody move. It's looking at us."
monologue: [welcome] Thank you, thank you! Sit down, we've got a fantastic show, assuming the power holds.
[crowd] Big crowd tonight. Or it was. We lost a few during the metal detector portion.
[traffic] Did everyone survive the commute? Traffic was backed up six blocks after somebody hacked the crossing lights to advertise noodles.
[crimestats] Corporate Security says crime is down again. Apparently they stopped counting anything that happens outside corporate property.
[pharmacy] I stopped by a pharmacy today. They've started locking up the bottled water. The cybernetic organs? Still self-service.
[mugging] You know times are tough when the mugger accepts store credit.
[landlord] My landlord says the building is structurally sound. Turns out that's a completely different thing from "safe."
[mentalhealth] The city announced a new mental health initiative. It's a billboard that says "Have you considered being richer?"
[rebrand] They renamed my district again. It's now "Opportunity Basin." Same craters, better font.
[ticket] I got a parking ticket today. For a car I don't own. In a district I've never been to. The Machine is very thorough.
[rain] Weather service says it's going to rain tomorrow. They didn't say water. They were very careful not to say water.
[transit] The transit authority added a new express line. It's the same line, but now it doesn't stop for the people who fall in.
[hospital] Great news from the hospital: they've reduced wait times by simply removing the chairs.
[surface] A man tried to sell me a map to the surface today. I said, "Buddy, I've seen the surface." He said, "Then you know why I'm selling the map."
[machine] The Machine wished everyone a happy productivity quarter today. It does not know what happiness is. It's very confident about it anyway.
[rent] Rent went up again. My landlord calls it "market rate." The market is a hole in the ground and the rate is everything you have.
[soylent] I tried the new soylent flavor. It's called "Original." I asked original what. They stopped returning my calls.
[dmv] Somebody firebombed the DMV today and honestly the lines moved faster.
[mayor] The mayor gave a speech about hope. Then the teleprompter caught fire, which, frankly, was the more honest part.
[tower] They opened a new luxury tower downtown. Forty floors. The elevator only goes up. Think about that.
[billboard] I saw a billboard for a class-action lawsuit against a billboard. We've achieved something here, folks.
[bank] The bank called to say my account was compromised. I said by whom. They said by the bank. At least they're honest now.
[warranty] Undermarket's booming. You can buy anything down there. I bought a warranty. It came with a warning label about the warranty.
[mascot] Public transit unveiled a new safety mascot. It's a skeleton. It waves. Nobody approved this and nobody can stop it.
[air] They say the air quality is "moderate" today. Moderate means you can see the person mugging you.
[gym] I joined a gym. It's just a room where they charge you to feel bad, so, you know, same as everywhere else.
[loyalty] Corporate rolled out a loyalty program. You give them loyalty, and in exchange they remember your name while they do it.
[lottery] The lottery jackpot hit a record high tonight. The odds also hit a record high. Those are the same number now.
[drone] A drone delivered my mail today, then asked for a tip, then filed a complaint about me. I've never felt so seen.
[newsanchor] The news anchor cried on air tonight. Ratings went up. They've made it a segment now. It's called "The Weather."
[doctor] My doctor told me to reduce stress. I asked how. He looked out the window for a while and then just quietly left.
[dating] There's a new dating app in the Basin. You match based on who owes the same people money. It's called Mutual.
[water] Good news, folks: the city says the water's safe to drink now. They didn't say for whom.
[tax] I got a letter from the tax office today. It was addressed to "Occupant or Next of Kin." They're just covering their bases.
[facerec] The Machine rolled out facial recognition downtown. Great system. It recognized my face and immediately asked if I was sure.
[statue] They put up a statue of the founder in the plaza. It's already been stolen twice. That's the most honest tribute you could pay the man.
[securitydoor] My building installed a new security door. It locks perfectly. From the inside. We're all still in there. Say hi to my family.
[clinic] The clinic offered me a loyalty card. Ten checkups and the eleventh organ failure is free.
[layoffs] The corporates announced record profits and record layoffs on the same day. They're calling it "efficiency." I'm calling it from a payphone, because they took my line.
[lemonade] I saw a kid selling lemonade on the corner. Then a licensing drone shut him down. Then the drone bought the stand. That kid's going to run this city someday, if it's still here.
[subway] The subway added a "quiet car." It's quiet because the speakers are broken and so is the door and so are we.
[horoscope] My horoscope said today was a good day to take risks. My horoscope has never been outside. My horoscope doesn't know about the district.
[heatwave] They're calling this the worst heat wave in fifty years. Fifty years ago they said the same thing. We've been winning that award every year. Consistency.
[permit] I applied for a permit to complain about permits. It's under review. The review is also under review.
[birthday] The Machine sent everyone a birthday message today. Everyone. Same day. It has decided we all have the same birthday now. It's easier for the servers.
[hiring] I passed a "Now Hiring" sign at a place that burned down last week. That's not optimism, that's the market. Somebody's already hiring for the fire.
[crimestats] The news said the crime rate dropped forty percent. Turns out they just moved the border of the district forty percent inward. We're all outside now.
[smokedetector] I bought a smoke detector. It went off immediately and hasn't stopped. I checked. No fire. It just knows something. I trust it now. We're friends.
[charity] A charity came to my door asking for donations to fight poverty. I said I'd love to help but I AM the poverty. They gave ME a leaflet. Full circle.
[mayor] The mayor promised to fix the potholes. Then he fell in one. We haven't seen him since. Honestly, best he's polled in years.
[robotdog] My neighbor got a robot dog. It guards the apartment, walks itself, and last week it unionized. Now it guards the apartment forty hours a week with breaks.
[museum] They opened a museum of the old world. One exhibit. It's a working light switch. There's a two-hour line. People weep.
[subscription] I tried to cancel a subscription today. The retention specialist cried. Then I cried. Then we agreed to see other services.
[air] Corporate wellness sent me a meditation app. It reminds me to breathe. Then it reminds me the air is a premium feature. Then it upsells me the good air.
[foreclosure] The bank foreclosed on a building, then the building foreclosed on the bank. Nobody knows who owns the block now. The block seems happy about it.
[worse] Somebody asked me if things could get worse. I said absolutely, and then, out of professional courtesy, I didn't elaborate.

[insurance] My insurer wrote to say my policy now excludes acts of God, acts of Corporate, and acts that are "frankly indistinguishable." That last clause took a lawyer three years and it's the truest thing anybody wrote this decade.
[funeral] A funeral home downtown is offering a payment plan. Twelve months. They do not check whether you make it to month twelve. That's the plan. That IS the plan.
[chrome] Fella at the bar showed me his new arm. Financed. Eighteen percent. Every time he waves at somebody it costs him money, so he's very selective about who he's pleased to see now.
[optics] My neighbor got the discount optics. They work beautifully. Every third thing he looks at has a coupon on it. He proposed to his wife and a burger appeared.
[dentist] Went to a dentist in the Basin last week. He is not a dentist. He is very good, though. That's the part that keeps me up.
[barber] The barbershop on my block does haircuts and minor surgery now. Same chair, same man, same question: "How short?"
[laundry] The laundromat put up a sign. "Not responsible for garments, contents, or outcomes." Outcomes. I have been thinking about outcomes all week.

[plumbing] My building's plumbing finally got fixed. Turns out it was never broken, it was rerouted. Somebody upstairs has been showering in my water pressure for six years, and honestly, good for him.
[elevator] The elevator in my building talks now. It says "Going up." It has never said going down. We've all quietly agreed not to raise it.
[grid] The power went out on my floor for nine hours. The grid called it a load-balancing event. I was the load. I was balanced.

[pirateradio] There's a pirate station broadcasting on the emergency band. All they play is weather from thirty years ago. It's the most soothing thing in this city and they'll shut it down by spring.
[tourism] The district launched a tourism campaign this week. The slogan is "Coldwater: You're Already Here."
[selfcheckout] The corner store went full self-checkout. No staff, no cashier, just you, the machine, and the machine's opinion of you.
[vendingmachine] A vending machine downtown has started accepting apologies. Not credits. Apologies. Fairest transaction I've had all year.
[escalator] They put an escalator in the transit hub. It's been broken since the day it opened, which makes it stairs, which makes it the only thing in this city doing its job.
[rats] The rats in my building have organized. Not unionized. Organized. There's a difference and I learned it the hard way and I'd rather not go into it.

[pigeons] Corporate built surveillance drones shaped like pigeons so they'd blend in. The pigeons noticed within a day. There's a war on now. I'm not taking sides publicly, but the pigeons are winning.
[stray] There's a stray cat in my alley with a bionic paw. Nobody knows where she got it. Nobody asks her. She's doing better than I am.
[school] The school by the Yards added a new subject this term. It's called Consent Forms. It isn't part of the curriculum. It IS the curriculum.
[wedding] Went to a wedding in the Basin last week. Beautiful ceremony. Both of them had to sign a non-compete.
[divorce] My cousin's divorce was settled by an algorithm. It awarded the apartment to the algorithm.
[neighbor] My neighbor plays music through the wall at three in the morning. I finally knocked. He apologized, turned it down, and asked whether I could hear the screaming better now.
[holiday] Corporate declared a new public holiday. It's unpaid, attendance is mandatory, and it's called Gratitude Day.
[joblisting] I saw a listing for entry level, ten years experience, must supply own oxygen. Forty applicants. I counted. I nearly made it forty-one.
[jobinterview] A friend of mine had a job interview. They asked where he sees himself in five years. He said "alive," and they wrote it down like it was ambitious.
[pension] The pension office sent me my retirement projection. It's a photograph of a hole.
[credit] My credit score went up eleven points this month. I asked why. They said good behavior. I don't know what I did and I'm now terrified of stopping.
[debt] I got a call from a debt collector representing another debt collector. They're eating each other out there. Give it a month and the whole problem solves itself.
[atm] The ATM on my corner charges a fee to tell you your balance, and a bigger fee if the balance is bad. It calls that "context."
[bankapp] The bank's app congratulates you when you save money. It has never congratulated me. Last week it sent a wellness check.
[casino] The casino's put in a machine that pays out in job offers. People still play it. That's the part that keeps me awake.
[deadball] Went to a Deadball game Saturday. Nine innings, four ambulances, and the crowd cheered exactly once, and it was not for anything that happened on the field.
[clusterpuck] I watched a Cluster Puck match. I don't understand the rules. Neither do they. They've replaced the referee twice, once mid-period and once mid-sentence.
[supplement] There's a supplement going round the gym called Yield. Makes you stronger. Also makes you agreeable. Nobody's asking about the second part, and I think that's the supplement talking.
[diet] New diet in the district: eat whatever you want, then worry about it. They're calling it a lifestyle. I've been on it thirty years.
[restaurant] A place opened downtown where the menu changes based on what the kitchen found that day. There's a rating system. Tonight it's a four.
[coffee] Real coffee's up again. The kind grown in dirt, by hands. It is now cheaper to buy the MEMORY of coffee, which they sell, which is legal, and which we have all apparently decided is fine.
[noodles] The noodle place on Fifth has a sign that says "All Meat Is Meat." I've read it forty times. It gets worse every time and I keep eating there.
[waterbill] My water bill came with a note thanking me for my conservation. I haven't had water since spring. Apparently that's what winning looks like.

[recycling] The city started a recycling program. You sort your waste into six bins, then a truck comes and puts all six in the same hole. But you sorted it. That's the civic part. That's your contribution.
[sewers] They're calling the sewer system "underutilized real estate" now. There are people living down there. Corporate refers to them as early tenants.
[realestate] A realtor showed me a studio with a window. An actual window, with an outside behind it. I cried. She raised the price. Honestly, fair.
[holding] Holding's overcrowded again, so they've started releasing people alphabetically. My last name starts with an A. I've never felt luckier or more nervous.
[bodycam] Corporate Security got new body cameras. They record everything. The footage goes to Corporate Security. Airtight system. No notes.
[lawyer] My lawyer says I have a very strong case. My lawyer also says he is not a lawyer. I'm choosing to focus on the first part.
[jury] I got called for jury duty. The verdict was already printed. They just needed twelve people to hold it.
[camera] There's a camera on my street pointed at another camera. I've watched them for a week. Neither has blinked. Something is happening there and I don't believe it involves us.
[assistant] My apartment has an assistant now. It listens for emergencies. Last night I sneezed and it asked whether I'd like to speak to a representative about my life.
[terms] I read a terms-of-service agreement all the way through this week. Page forty says I have agreed to be "reasonably surprised." That's the entire clause. That's all it says.
[passwords] Corporate made everyone change their passwords. New rules: twelve characters, one symbol, and it cannot be anything you actually believe.
[maintenance] The Machine went down for maintenance for six minutes yesterday. Six minutes. Crime dropped, the trains ran, and a man in the Yards reported feeling briefly optimistic.
[photograph] Somebody found a photograph of the old skyline. We all stood round looking at it. Then someone pointed out the sky was a different color, and we all went home.

[cleanrain] It rained clean water in the north district for eleven minutes on Tuesday. Nobody knows why. Two hundred people stood outside with their mouths open like idiots. I was one of them. I'd do it again tomorrow.
[radiation] My doctor says my rad count is "within range." I asked whose range. He said it's a big range. It is a very big range, folks.
[mutation] A man on my block grew a third arm this spring. Everyone has been extremely polite about it, which is the most Coldwater thing I have ever seen. Three arms, and not one question.
[cloning] The clone clinic's got a special on this month. Two for one. Sit with that. Think about who walks in wanting that.
[memories] They sell memory implants now. Real ones, off real people. I tried a demo. It was somebody's Tuesday. Nothing happened in it. Best day I've had in years.
[dreamshop] There's a shop selling dreams by the hour. I asked for something with a beach. They gave me a beach. There was a fence.
[insomnia] I haven't slept properly in eleven years. My doctor calls it insomnia. I call it paying attention.
[therapy] Therapy's covered by corporate now. Six sessions, and the therapist is an employee of the thing you're upset about. It's efficient. It isn't therapy, but it's efficient.
[church] The Church of the Reasonable Refund opened a second location. Same god, better parking.

[gala] There was a charity gala downtown for the district's poor. Tickets were nine hundred credits. The poor were not invited, on the grounds that they couldn't afford it, and everyone agreed that was ironic, and nobody agreed to do anything about it.
[awards] Corporate held an awards ceremony for itself last night. Nineteen categories. It swept.
[survey] The hospital sent me a satisfaction survey. Question one: how likely are you to recommend this experience. Well. I'm still here, so: cautiously.
[warrantycard] I found the warranty card in my new heater. The warranty is void if the unit is used. Not misused. Used.
[heater] My heater has two settings. Off, and a sound.
[mirrorglass] The tower across from mine put in mirrored glass so nobody can see in. Now I just watch myself watching them. Six months of that. We've grown close.
[smog] The smog was so thick this morning I walked into a wall, and the wall apologized. Somebody is already charging for that. I guarantee it.
[roadsign] There's a sign out on the Deadleg road that says HELP IS 40 MILES. It does not say in which direction. I have thought about that sign more than I have thought about my own family.

[hauler] I met a hauler who runs the void road. Twelve hours out, twelve hours back, no radio. I asked what he thinks about out there. He said "the road." I gave him nine more minutes to add something to that. It's the road.

[flying] A man at the airfield offered me a flight over the Basin for two hundred credits. I said what's the catch. He said there's no catch, there's no landing gear. We both laughed. Then only one of us was laughing.
[forecast] The forecast has said "clear" for six days running. Last night the forecaster stood outside and said "clear" while visibly in weather. That is not incompetence, folks. That's commitment.
[acidrain] It rained out in the Scarletwastes last week and three people's coats are still fizzing. The coat shop is calling it a finish.
[fishing] They reopened the fishing pier. The fish are back. They are not exactly fish anymore, but they're back, the pier's open, people are happy, and I am not going to be the one who ruins it.
[bird] I saw a bird this morning. A real one. It looked at me with what I can only describe as disappointment, and then it left, and I have been thinking about it all day.
newsjoke: And now for the news. Tonight's top story: "{headline}." I'd unpack that, but the last man who unpacked it is still in Holding.
You see the headline tonight? "{headline}." I read it twice. It got worse the second time.
Here's one for you: "{headline}." Somewhere, an executive is calling that a growth opportunity.
Big news tonight, folks: "{headline}." And they say nothing ever happens in this city.
The headline going around tonight is "{headline}." I called the newsroom to confirm it. They laughed and hung up. So: confirmed.
Real story tonight: "{headline}." My producer says I can't comment on it. My producer is also under the desk, so.
Top of the news: "{headline}." You can't make this up. Believe me, legal already asked if I had.
Tonight in the news: "{headline}." And the terrifying part is that's the GOOD news.
Made the wire today: "{headline}." Somewhere the Machine filed that under "within acceptable parameters."
Here's the story everyone's talking about: "{headline}." Well. Everyone still able to talk.
News just in: "{headline}." I'd say you couldn't script it, but somebody clearly did, and they're getting paid more than me.
The big headline tonight: "{headline}." I'm told the mayor has no comment, which, for once, is the smartest thing he's said all year.
Straight from the feed: "{headline}." I showed it to the band. The band asked to go home. The band cannot go home.
Tonight's headline: "{headline}." Frame that one, folks. In this city, that's what passes for a historical document.
open: From somewhere above the smog and only slightly outside the blast radius... it's The Tonight Show!
Live from a studio that passed its last safety inspection under a different administration. It's The Tonight Show!
Coming to you on the one channel Corporate Security hasn't seized yet. It's The Tonight Show!
Broadcasting into your skull whether you asked for it or not: ladies, gentlemen, and legally-distinct entities, it's The Tonight Show!
Transmitting live on the frequency they SWORE they'd jammed. It's The Tonight Show!
From the last building on the block with working lights, most of them. It's The Tonight Show!
Beamed to you at great personal risk to everyone involved. It's The Tonight Show!
It's late, you're awake, and something's wrong. That can only mean it's The Tonight Show!
Rebuilt after the fire, rewired after the flood, and back on the air out of pure spite. It's The Tonight Show!
The only program in the district legally classified as both entertainment and a hazard. It's The Tonight Show!
Airing tonight because the injunction doesn't take effect until midnight. It's The Tonight Show!
Filmed before a live studio audience, most of whom are here voluntarily. It's The Tonight Show!
Powered by one generator and a great deal of denial. It's The Tonight Show!
Still standing where the map says there's a crater. It's The Tonight Show!
settle: Okay. Okay! Sit down, you'll hurt yourselves. Some of you already have.
Thank you. Please. Save some of that for the end, you'll want it then.
All right, that's plenty. The applause sign's broken, you're doing this on your own and I'm touched.
Please, sit, sit. The fire marshal's in tonight and he's already counting.
Thank you! You're very kind. You're very loud. Pick one, we've got a show to do.
Easy, easy. That's a lot of noise for people who know what's coming.
Settle down, I know, I know. I'd clap too if I'd made it here.
sidekick_aside: That's the one you told at rehearsal, {host_first}. It didn't work then either.
I laughed. I want that on the record. Somebody had to.
The band would like it noted that they are contractually forbidden from reacting to that.
Legally I have to remind the audience that laughter is voluntary.
{host_first}, the sponsors just turned the applause sign off manually. That's a first.
I've heard that joke in three districts now and it's wanted in two of them.
Beautiful. No notes. Well, all notes, but no time.
For those at home, {host_first} is now doing the little bow he does when he's stalling.
I'd like the audience to know I begged him to cut that one.
That joke is now evidence, {host_first}. I'm just the announcer, but I know evidence.
The band wants hazard pay after that, and honestly, so do I.
For the folks at home, that silence is the sound of {host_first} realizing what he said.
We are contractually one more of those away from a warning label, {host_first}.
I'm laughing. It's a survival response, but I'm laughing.
Nineteen years I've announced this man. That was in the bottom four.
I'm required to say the views expressed are his. Loudly. Twice, tonight.
The teleprompter skipped that one on purpose, {host_first}. It's been right before.
Somewhere a lawyer just woke up and doesn't know why.
I've started keeping a list. That one goes near the top, and the list is not a good list.
The crew has voted. It was close. You lost, {host_first}.
signoff: That's all the time we've got tonight. Huge thanks to {guest} for surviving the segment.
Thanks to {guest}, thanks to the band, and thanks to whoever's keeping the generator running.
Remember: if somebody offers you free cyberware in an alley, at least ask if it comes with a warranty.
Get home safe, and if you can't get home, get somewhere with a door.
Goodnight, everybody. You've been a wonderful audience, and statistically, most of you will be back.
That's our show. Tip your bouncer, hydrate your fear, and we'll see you tomorrow. Probably.
Thanks again to {guest}. From all of us up here on the last lit stage in the district, goodnight.
That's it for tonight. Be kind to each other, or at least be quiet about it. Goodnight!
We're out of time and nearly out of power. Thanks to {guest}, and to you, for being awake. Goodnight.
Remember, folks: it's a hard city, but it's the only one that's still on the air. Goodnight from The Tonight Show.
That's our show. Lock your door, salt your soylent, and we'll do it all again tomorrow, grid permitting.
Thanks to {guest}, and to you, for choosing us over the several emergencies happening outside. Goodnight.
We're out of time. Be suspicious, be kind, and never in that order. Goodnight, everybody.
That's all from the last lit desk in the district. Thanks to {guest}. Sleep with one eye open; it's cheaper than a security system.
Goodnight, folks. If the lights come back on, thank the generator. If they don't, thank you for watching in the dark.
Huge thanks to {guest} for making it out alive, and to the rest of you for making it in. Goodnight from The Tonight Show.
tease: Tonight: corporate executives explain why exploding vending machines are actually a premium feature.
Tonight: a local street chef prepares something the lawyers have asked us to call "food."
Tonight: we meet a man who has legally declared his apartment an independent nation, and the tanks are already massing.
Tonight: the weather, the news, and a surprising amount of blood, all before the second commercial.
Tonight: one lucky audience member goes home with a prize, and the other four hundred go home with radiation sickness.
Tonight: science, culture, and a segment our insurer specifically told us not to air.
Tonight: we answer the question on everyone's mind: is it a leak, or is it a feature? The answer will not comfort you.
Tonight: a very special guest, a very ordinary catastrophe, and the band, if they've sobered up.
Tonight: celebrity gossip, from the two celebrities we have left.
Tonight: we test whether the studio audience can be replaced with cardboard. Results are inconclusive and litigious.
Tonight: heartwarming stories, market updates, and the slow collapse of everything, in that order.
Tonight: an interview so candid our sponsors have already fled the building.
Tonight: a man who's never been right about anything predicts your future, and you'll pay attention anyway.
Tonight: we count the exits, we count the survivors, and if the numbers match, we've had a good show.
Tonight: a guest, a scandal, and the exact amount of legal exposure our producers will allow.
Tonight: the Machine has an announcement, the grid has an opinion, and neither of them asked you.
Tonight: free samples, in the sense that nobody agreed to pay for what's about to happen.
Tonight: one guest tells the truth, and we find out live whether the building can survive it.
Tonight: we reunite a man with the toaster that made him rich. There will not be a dry eye or a working outlet.
Tonight: everything's fine, nothing's fine, and somewhere in between there's a musical number.
